title: Seasons: how plants, animals and people change through the year

summary.text: Every year in India, the hot months, the rains and the cool months come round again in the same order. These parts of the year are called seasons. Summer is hotter because the midday Sun is higher, so its light falls more straight down and is packed into a smaller patch of ground. Plants, animals and people all change with the seasons. Many trees drop their leaves in the dry months, frogs breed in monsoon puddles, ducks fly in from Central Asia for the winter, and families switch to cotton, buttermilk and mangoes in summer. In this unit you pull a hidden yellow colour out of a green leaf, and find out why leaves turn yellow before they fall.
summary.art: A round picture split into three parts: a hot summer street in Chennai with a mango seller and a neer mor pot, a monsoon street with umbrellas and frogs in a puddle, and a cool winter morning with a kolam, a shawl and ducks on a lake.

intro.hook: A neem tree is dropping yellow leaves in March, the hottest, driest time of year. A week later, the same tree is covered in soft new leaves. Is the tree sick, or does she know something?
intro.text: The neem tree is not sick. She is changing with the season, the way you change into cotton clothes in summer. In this unit you look out of your window for signs of the season. You find a colour hiding inside a green leaf. You use a torch to see why summer sunlight is stronger. And you meet the koel, the frog, the pintail duck, the farmer and the fisher, who all change what they do as the year turns.
intro.art: A neem tree beside a block of flats, half her branches bare with yellow leaves falling and half with fresh light-green leaves and tiny white flowers, and a girl watching from a balcony.

outcomes: I can name India's seasons, say which months they come in where I live, and give one clue for each.
I can explain why summer is hotter than winter, using the torch test: straight light is packed into a smaller patch.
I can describe how plants change with the seasons, and explain why many trees drop their leaves in the dry months.
I can separate the colours in a leaf on a paper strip, and use my result to explain why leaves turn yellow before they fall.
I can give examples of animals that change with the seasons, and say what problem each change solves for them.
I can describe how people change their clothes, food, work and festivals with the seasons.
I can tell how Garner and Allard found that plants measure the length of the day to know the season.

terms.meaning: A part of the year with its own kind of weather, which comes back at about the same time every year.
terms.example: In Chennai, the hot season comes every year from about March to June.
terms.art: A calendar with the months coloured in three bands: orange for summer, blue for the rains, pale green for the cool months.

terms.meaning: The hottest season. In most of India it comes from about March to June.
terms.example: In May in Hyderabad, the afternoon can be hotter than 40 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A bright midday street with very short shadows and people under umbrellas for shade.

terms.meaning: A wind that changes direction with the seasons and brings the rains. People also call the rainy season itself the monsoon.
terms.example: The south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around the first of June.
terms.art: Dark clouds rolling in from the sea over the coconut palms of a Kerala beach.

terms.meaning: The rains that come to Tamil Nadu and nearby places from about October to December, when the winds blow from the north-east.
terms.example: Chennai gets most of its rain in October, November and December.
terms.art: A wet Chennai street in November with a child in a raincoat stepping round a puddle.

terms.meaning: The coolest season. In most of India it comes from about December to February.
terms.example: On a January night in Delhi it can be colder than 5 degrees Celsius, while in Chennai it stays near 20.
terms.art: A foggy Delhi morning with people in sweaters next to a sunny Chennai morning with a girl in a light shawl.

terms.meaning: The old Sanskrit word for a season. The old Indian calendar splits the year into six ritus of about two months each.
terms.example: Vasanta ritu is spring, and Varsha ritu is the rainy season.
terms.art: A ring of six coloured parts, each with a small picture: flowers, hot sun, rain, clear sky, cool mist and cold.

terms.meaning: A deciduous tree drops all or most of their leaves for part of the year, and then grows new ones.
terms.example: A teak tree drops their big leaves in the dry months and grows new ones before the rains.
terms.art: A teak tree with bare branches and a carpet of big brown leaves on the ground below.

terms.meaning: An evergreen plant keeps green leaves all year. Old leaves fall a few at a time, and new ones keep growing.
terms.example: A coconut palm is green all year round.
terms.art: A coconut palm, green and full, next to a bare deciduous tree in the dry season.

terms.meaning: The green colouring in leaves. Plants use it to catch sunlight and make their food.
terms.example: A palak leaf is dark green because she has a lot of chlorophyll.
terms.art: A close-up of a green leaf with tiny green dots inside its cells.

terms.meaning: A substance that gives something its colour.
terms.example: Turmeric has a yellow pigment that stains your fingers.
terms.art: A row of things with their pigments: turmeric, a green leaf, a red chilli and a carrot.

terms.meaning: The things a living body needs to grow and stay healthy, apart from water and air.
terms.example: Plants take nutrients such as nitrogen from the soil, through their roots.
terms.art: A plant with arrows showing nutrients moving up from the soil into the roots and stem.

terms.meaning: A long journey that animals make every year, at the same season, to find food, warmth or a safe place for their young.
terms.example: Northern pintail ducks fly from Central Asia to the lakes of India every winter.
terms.art: A line of ducks flying over snowy mountains towards a lake with lotus leaves.

terms.meaning: A long, deep sleep through the cold months, when an animal's body slows right down and they live on stored fat.
terms.example: Some Himalayan black bears sleep in a den through the snowy winter.
terms.art: A black bear curled up asleep in a rocky den with snow outside.

terms.meaning: How many hours of daylight there are, from sunrise to sunset. It changes through the year.
terms.example: In Delhi, the longest day in June has about 14 hours of daylight, and the shortest in December has about 10.
terms.art: Two clocks side by side, one with a long yellow arc of daylight for June, one with a shorter arc for December.

terms.meaning: Gathering a crop when it is ready.
terms.example: Rice is harvested in many parts of Tamil Nadu in January, and Pongal celebrates it.
terms.art: Women and men cutting golden rice in a field, with sheaves stacked by the bund.

terms.meaning: An imaginary line through the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole. The Earth spins round it. The Earth's axis is tilted, and this tilt is what gives us seasons.
terms.example: A spinning top that leans a little to one side spins round a tilted axis.
terms.art: A globe on a stand, tilted, with a dotted line running through it from top to bottom.

explanations.definition: A season is a part of the year with its own kind of weather. The seasons come round in the same order every year.
explanations.description: The year goes round like a wheel. In most of India, it gets hotter from March, and May is often the hottest month. Then the rains come, from about June to September. After the rains, the air gets cooler and drier, and December and January are the coolest months. Then it warms up again. The order is the same every year. The exact dates change a little from year to year, and they change a lot from place to place.
examples: Every year, mangoes come to the market in about April and May.
Every year, the rains reach Kerala first, around the first of June, and spread north over the next five or six weeks.
Every year, the mornings in December are cooler than the mornings in May.
explanations.art: A wheel of twelve months with summer, the rains and the cool months coloured round it, and small pictures of a mango, an umbrella and a shawl.
explanations.context: This card says what a season is, and why the seasons come back every year in the same order.

explanations.definition: The India Meteorological Department, which watches India's weather, counts four seasons: winter (January and February), summer (March to May), the south-west monsoon (June to September) and the post-monsoon season (October to December).
explanations.description: People split the year in different ways. The weather department uses four seasons. The old Indian calendar uses six ritus of about two months each: Vasanta (spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (the rains), Sharad (early autumn), Hemanta (the cool time before winter) and Shishira (winter). Old Tamil poems also count six seasons, such as kaar, the rainy season. Many people simply say summer, rainy season and winter. None of these is the one true count. They are different ways of cutting up the same year. The seasons are also different in different places. Most of India gets most of its rain from June to September, from the south-west monsoon. But Chennai gets most of its rain from October to December, from the north-east monsoon. Delhi has a cold winter, with foggy mornings. Kochi and Chennai stay warm all year, so there the rains mark the seasons more than the cold does.
examples: In Kochi, the big rains start in June. In Chennai, the biggest rains come in November.
Vasanta ritu is the time of Holi in the north and Ugadi in the south.
In Srinagar it can snow in January. In Thiruvananthapuram it never does.
explanations.art: A map of India with small weather pictures: snow in Kashmir, fog over Delhi, rain clouds over Kerala in June, and rain clouds over Chennai in November.
explanations.context: How many seasons does India have? This card shows that people count them in different ways, and that each place has its own pattern.

explanations.concept: Why summer is hotter than winter
explanations.definition: In summer, the midday Sun is higher in the sky, so its light falls more straight down and is packed into a smaller patch of ground. The days are also longer. Both make the ground warmer.
explanations.description: Remember the torch test. When the torch shone straight down, its light made a small, bright patch. When it shone at a slant, the same light spread over a much bigger patch, so each square got less. Sunlight works the same way. In summer, the midday Sun in India is high, nearly overhead, and your shadow at noon is very short. Each patch of ground gets a lot of light. In winter, the midday Sun is lower in the sky, and your noon shadow is longer. The same sunlight is spread over more ground, so each patch warms less. The days are shorter in winter too, so there are fewer hours of sunshine. Why does the Sun climb higher in some months? Because the Earth's axis is tilted. For part of the year, our half of the Earth leans towards the Sun. Six months later, it leans away. You will learn more about the tilt in Class 5. Many people think summer comes when the Earth is closest to the Sun. But the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during India's winter.
examples: At noon in Chennai in May, your shadow is so short it hides under your feet.
At noon in Delhi in December, your shadow is about as long as you are tall, or a little longer.
Kerala and Tamil Nadu are close to the equator, where the Sun is high all year. That is why their winters are mild.
explanations.art: Two pictures of the same street at noon: in May, the Sun high overhead and short shadows. In December, the Sun lower in the south and longer shadows.
explanations.context: Why is May so hot and December so cool, when it is the same Sun? This card explains, using the torch test.

explanations.concept: Why many trees drop their leaves in the dry months
explanations.definition: A deciduous tree drops their leaves for part of the year. In most of India, they do this in the hot, dry months before the rains. Before a leaf falls, the tree breaks down the green chlorophyll and takes useful nutrients back into the branches. The yellow colour that was hidden under the green then shows.
explanations.description: Leaves lose water all the time, through tiny holes underneath. In the rains, the soil is wet, and the roots easily replace that water. From about February to May, many places get almost no rain, and the soil dries out. A big tree with thousands of leaves could lose more water than her roots can find. So trees such as teak, peepal, neem, gulmohar and the Indian almond drop many or all of their leaves. A leaf is full of useful nutrients, such as nitrogen, that the tree took from the soil. Throwing them away would be a waste. So before the leaf falls, the tree breaks down the green chlorophyll and moves much of the nitrogen back into the branches, to use for new leaves. Your strip test showed that a green leaf also holds yellow pigments. They stay in the leaf longer than the green does. So as the green goes, the leaf turns yellow. Some trees, such as the Indian almond, also make new red colours in their leaves before they drop them. Then, often before the rains, new leaves come out, soft and pale green or coppery pink.
examples: The peepal tree drops their leaves for a short time in the dry season. Their new leaves come out coppery pink.
Neem trees drop many old leaves around February and March. By Ugadi, they have new leaves and tiny white flowers, used in Ugadi pachadi.
Coconut palms and mango trees are evergreen. They never stand bare.
explanations.art: A teak tree in three stages: green in the rains, yellow and dropping leaves in the dry season, and bare with a few new leaves just before the monsoon.
explanations.context: Why does a tree drop leaves in the hottest, driest months? And why do the leaves turn yellow first? This card explains, using the strip test.

explanations.definition: Many plants sense the length of the night, and use it to know the time of year. When the nights reach the right length, they start to flower. This is called photoperiodism.
explanations.description: A plant cannot read a calendar, but the length of the night is a very good clock. It changes the same way every year, whatever the weather does. Plants sense light with special substances in their leaves. They notice how long the dark lasts each night. Some plants, such as the chrysanthemum, or sevanthi, flower when the nights get long, in the cool months. That is why sevanthi garlands are cheap in November and December. Other plants flower when the nights get short. Scientists found this in the 1920s, as the story of Garner and Allard tells. Plants also notice warmth, cold and rain. Many seeds wait in the dry soil and sprout only after the first rains. Plants feel, remember and decide, and choosing when to flower is one of their biggest decisions. Some scientists call this an automatic response, built into the plant by their genes.
examples: Sevanthi, the chrysanthemum, flowers in the long nights of the cool months.
Some old rice varieties flower at the same time every year, in October or November, even when farmers sow them at different times.
After the first rains, grass sprouts on bare ground within a few days.

perspectives.explanation: Plants sense the night and make a choice about when to flower. Their senses and signals are real, and their choice is theirs.
The flowering is set off by a chain of chemical changes, and it is best called an automatic response, not a choice.

explanations.art: A sevanthi plant in a pot with a moon and a long dark night drawn above, and a bunch of yellow sevanthi flowers in a market basket.
explanations.context: How does a plant know when to flower? This card explains how plants use the length of the night.

explanations.concept: How animals change with the seasons
explanations.definition: Animals change what they do, where they live and sometimes how their bodies look as the seasons change. Each change helps them with a problem that season brings, such as heat, cold, dry food or a safe time for their young.
explanations.description: Each season brings its own problems and chances. In summer, water is short and the afternoons are very hot. Buffaloes have fewer sweat glands than cows, so they lie in mud or water to cool off. The koel calls loudly from March to June. This is her breeding time, and she lays her eggs in crows' nests, which are busy then too. The monsoon fills puddles and ponds. Frogs need water for their eggs and tadpoles, so they call and lay eggs after the first heavy rains. Winged termites fly out of the ground after the first rains, looking for a place to start a new colony. In winter, lakes in Central Asia and Siberia freeze, and the food under the water is locked under ice. So ducks such as the northern pintail fly thousands of kilometres to India's lakes, and fly back in spring. In the Himalayas, some black bears sleep in a den through the snowy months, living on their fat. Olive ridley turtles come ashore on Chennai and Odisha beaches from about January to March to lay their eggs.
examples: Openbill storks, egrets and other water birds fill Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary near Chennai from about November to March.
After the first big rain of the monsoon, winged termites fly round street lights at night.
On hot afternoons, crows sit with their beaks open to lose heat.
explanations.art: A season wheel of animals: a koel calling on a mango tree in summer, frogs in a monsoon puddle, ducks landing on a lake in winter, and a buffalo lying in mud.
explanations.context: Why does the koel call in summer, and why do ducks fly to India in winter? This card is about how animals change with the seasons.

explanations.concept: How people change with the seasons
explanations.definition: People change their clothes, food, homes, work and festivals with the seasons, to stay comfortable and to fit in with the plants and animals they depend on.
explanations.description: In summer, families wear loose cotton clothes and drink buttermilk, tender coconut water and panakam. They eat mangoes, watermelon and nungu, the ice apple of the palmyra palm. Many families dry vadams and make mango pickle on the terrace, because the strong sun dries food fast. In the rains, farmers sow rice and other crops, because the fields finally have enough water. Umbrellas and raincoats come out. In the cool months, people in the north wear sweaters, monkey caps and shawls, and sit in the sun at midday. Many festivals mark a harvest: Onam in Kerala in August or September, Pongal in Tamil Nadu and Makar Sankranti in January, and Baisakhi in Punjab in April. Even fishing changes. Every year the Government of India stops most fishing at sea for 61 days, while many fish breed. On the east coast this is from 15 April to 14 June. On the west coast it is from 1 June to 31 July.
examples: Jasmine flowers are plentiful in Madurai in summer, and costly in the cool months, when the plants make fewer.
Pongal is cooked with the new rice of the January harvest.
In Delhi in winter, people sell roasted sweet potatoes and peanuts on the street.
explanations.art: A family in three seasons: drinking buttermilk under a fan in summer, a girl with an umbrella and her mother sowing rice in the rains, and the family cooking Pongal in a pot outside on a cool January morning.
explanations.context: How does your family change through the year? This card is about how people change with the seasons.

explanations.description: Scientists agree that the Earth as a whole is getting warmer, mostly because people burn coal, oil and gas. In many countries, records kept for a hundred years or more show some plants flowering earlier in spring than they used to. In India, fewer such records exist, so scientists are still working out how much each season has shifted. Many farmers say the rains have become less regular, with long dry gaps and then very heavy downpours. Weather scientists are studying whether this is a lasting change. Nobody can yet say exactly how India's seasons will be in 50 years.
examples: Japan has kept records of when cherry trees flower in Kyoto for more than a thousand years. In recent decades, the flowering has come earlier.
Grandparents often remember cooler summers. Their memories are useful clues, but memory can be wrong, so scientists check them against written records.
explanations.art: A grandmother and a girl on a balcony looking at an old diary of flowering dates, with a mango tree in flower below.
explanations.context: Are the seasons the same as when your grandparents were small? This card says what scientists know and what they are still finding out.

agreed.text: The seasons come round in the same order every year.
agreed.evidence: Weather records kept in India since the 1800s show the same pattern every year: hot months, the rains, then cool months.

agreed.text: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis, not by the Earth's distance from the Sun.
agreed.evidence: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during India's winter. And when it is winter in India, it is summer in Australia, under the same Sun.

agreed.text: Sunlight falling straight down warms the ground more than sunlight falling at a slant.
agreed.evidence: In the torch test, slanting light spread the same light over many more squares. Measurements of sunshine on the ground show the same thing.

agreed.text: Green leaves hold yellow and orange pigments as well as green chlorophyll. Before a leaf falls, the chlorophyll breaks down first.
agreed.evidence: Paper strip tests separate the pigments. Scientists have also measured the pigments in leaves as they age.

agreed.text: Many plants use the length of the night to tell the season.
agreed.evidence: Garner and Allard made tobacco plants flower in summer by shutting them in the dark for part of each day. Many experiments since have shown the same with other plants.

challenging.claim: Summer comes when the Earth is closest to the Sun.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Being near a fire makes you warmer, so it seems the same should be true of the Sun.
challenging.against: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in India's winter. And Australia has summer while India has winter.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea of why summer is hot.

challenging.claim: A tree that drops their leaves in the dry season is dying or sick.
challenging.who: Many people who see a bare tree in March
challenging.for: Yellow leaves can be a sign of trouble, for example in a potted plant that gets too much water.
challenging.against: Deciduous trees drop their leaves every year and grow new ones. Before the leaves fall, the tree takes back useful nutrients from them.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a bare tree in the dry season is a sick tree.

challenging.claim: India really has six seasons, and the four-season count is wrong.
challenging.who: Some people who follow the old six-ritu calendar
challenging.for: The six ritus fit North India's year well, and people have used them for over two thousand years.
challenging.against: Seasons are a way people choose to split the year. The weather department's four seasons fit India's rainfall well. In Chennai or Kochi, three seasons may fit even better.
challenging.context: How many seasons does India have? This card shows that it depends on how you choose to count.

challenging.claim: The pied cuckoo, called the chataka in old Sanskrit poems, brings the monsoon to North India.
challenging.who: An old belief in many parts of India
challenging.for: Pied cuckoos fly in from Africa and are usually first heard in North India around the time the monsoon arrives.
challenging.against: The bird cannot make rain. Both the bird and the rain come with the same seasonal winds. Bird watchers are still studying how closely the bird's arrival matches the rain each year.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief that a bird brings the rain.

challenging.claim: Plants do not really know the season. They only react to light.
challenging.for: The steps by which a plant senses the night can be described as chemical changes.
challenging.against: Plants feel the length of the night, remember it over many nights, and choose when to flower. Sensing, remembering and choosing are what knowing is.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a plant knows the season.

big_questions.q: The yellow was inside the green leaf all along. What else might be hidden inside things we think we know well?
big_questions.hint: Think about the strip test, and what the green was covering.

big_questions.q: A tree takes back the useful parts of a leaf before letting it fall. Is the fallen leaf still part of the tree?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the nitrogen went, and what happens to the leaf on the ground.

big_questions.q: A plant measures the length of the night to know the season. How do you know what season it is?
big_questions.hint: Think of your clothes, your food, the sounds outside and the light.

big_questions.q: When it is summer in India, it is winter in Australia. So is there such a thing as 'the' season, for the whole Earth?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tilted Earth going round the Sun.

big_questions.q: Ducks fly thousands of kilometres to India every winter. Where is a migrating duck's real home?
big_questions.hint: Think about where she lays her eggs, and where she spends most of the year.

big_questions.q: Your grandparents' summers may have felt different from yours. How could we find out if the seasons are really changing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what records people could keep, year after year.

story.title: The Neem Tree Outside Our Window
story.note: The story is made up. Everything about the neem tree, the koel and the season is true: many neem trees drop old leaves in February and March, grow new leaves and flowers by Ugadi, and the koel starts calling in the hot months.
text: Our flat in Hyderabad is on the third floor, and our balcony looks straight into a neem tree. My name is Lakshmi. I am nine. My brother Arjun is six, and he thinks the neem tree belongs to him.
One morning in February, Arjun came running in from the balcony with his hands full of leaves. They were yellow, with brown spots.
"Akka, the tree is dying!" he said. "The leaves are falling off. We have to give her water."

He filled a steel tumbler at the kitchen tap and leaned over the balcony railing. The water splashed down onto the scooter parked below. Our Amamma, our grandmother, came out of the kitchen with a ladle in her hand.
"Arjun, the tree's roots go deeper than our building's water tank," she said. "Your tumbler will not help her. And Ravi garu's scooter is now very clean."
Arjun did not laugh. He looked at the leaves in his hand. "But why is she dropping them?"

I did not know. So I looked carefully at the tree. Some branches were still green. Others had a lot of yellow leaves, and some were nearly bare. Under the tree, the ground was covered in yellow leaves, and the sweeper aunty had made a pile of them by the gate.
"It hasn't rained since November," I said slowly. "The soil must be very dry."
"That is part of it," said Amamma. "Leaves drink up water all day long. In the dry months, a big tree cannot keep all of them full. So she lets the old ones go."
"But why are they yellow first?" asked Arjun. "Green leaves are good. Why do they turn yellow?"
Amamma smiled at me. "Lakshmi, you did that experiment last week. The one with the palak and the paper strip."

I remembered. Amma had helped me rub a palak leaf onto a strip of blotting paper with a coin, until there was a dark green line. Then we stood the strip in a little nail polish remover, in a tumbler with a plate on top. The liquid had climbed the paper, and the green line had spread out. Above it, near the top, there was a thin yellow stripe. A yellow colour from a green leaf.
"The yellow was inside the green leaf all along," I told Arjun. "You just can't see it, because the green is so strong. When a leaf gets old, the green goes away first. Then the yellow shows."
"Where does the green go?" Arjun asked.
This time Amamma answered. "The tree breaks the green down and takes the good things back into her branches. She keeps them for her new leaves. A tree does not waste."
Arjun thought about it. Then he picked out the yellowest leaf from his pile and held it up to the light. "So this leaf has already given her food back?"
"A lot of it," said Amamma.
We decided to watch the tree every morning. I drew her in my notebook on the first of each week, and Arjun counted the bare branches he could see from the balcony.
In the second week of March, the tree looked thin and tired. Arjun was worried again. But I had noticed something. At the tips of the bare twigs, there were tiny buds, reddish and soft.

By the third week, the buds had opened into new leaves. They were pale green and shiny, so soft that they hung down like little wet feathers. Then came the flowers, tiny and white, in bunches. The whole balcony smelled sweet and a little bitter.

On Ugadi morning, Amamma reached out from the balcony with a long stick and pulled a branch close. She picked a handful of neem flowers. She put them in the Ugadi pachadi, with new jaggery, raw mango, tamarind, salt and chilli.
"Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, hot and tangy," she said, giving us each a spoonful. "All the tastes of the year, for the new year."
The bitter came from the neem flowers. Arjun made a face. Then he went out onto the balcony and looked up at the tree for a long time.
"She wasn't dying," he said. "She was getting ready."
That evening, from somewhere high in the neem tree, a bird called. Ku-oo. Ku-oo. Louder each time, until it seemed to fill the whole street.
"The koel is back," said Amamma. "Now summer has really started."

I wrote it in my notebook, under the drawing of the tree with her new leaves. Week 6: new leaves, flowers, koel calling. Then I thought about the yellow stripe on the blotting paper. It had been hiding in a green leaf all along, waiting for the green to go.
story.epiphany: A tree that drops yellow leaves in the dry months is not dying. She takes back what is useful from her leaves, lets them fall, and grows new ones for the new season. The yellow was in the leaves all along.

Where did the yellow colour in the falling leaves come from?
Why did watching the tree every week help Lakshmi more than looking once?
Which tree near your home could you watch through the year?

Fishing boats stay tied up on the west coast in June and July. (Rainy season)
Mushrooms pop up in the park. (Rainy season)
Pintail ducks swim on the lake, far from Central Asia. (Winter)
Sevanthi garlands are cheap in the flower market. (Winter)

Coconut oil in Delhi has gone hard in the bottle. (Winter)

printables.title: A season wheel board with three parts: summer, rainy season, winter

rules: Shuffle the clue cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take a card and read the clue out loud, but not the answer in brackets.
The other players point to a season on the wheel board. Each right guess scores 1 point.
Anyone who can say why that clue belongs to that season scores 1 more point.
If you live in Tamil Nadu, remember your big rains come from October to December. If a card does not match your home, say why and score a point.
After all the cards are read, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the board. 2. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Each card is a clue about a season. Read it out, and we will guess the season.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read the clue. Others guess the season.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Season Am I?, a game of season clues.

flow.do: Play one practice card together.
flow.say: Practice card: frogs croak all night from the puddles. Which season? Why?
flow.kid: Frogs croak all night. Which season is it? Tap your answer.

check.q: Frogs croak all night from the puddles. Which season is it?
options: Summer
Rainy season
Winter
check.why: Frogs need water to lay their eggs, and the puddles fill in the rains. So frogs call and breed in the rainy season.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read cards. 2. Keep score.
flow.say: Your turn. Read your clue. Can anyone say why it belongs to that season, for an extra point?
flow.kid: Read your clue. Guess. Say why for an extra point.
flow.parent: Ask 'why' as often as you can. The reasons are the real learning: the frog needs water, the duck's lake has frozen, the strong sun dries the vadams.

flow.do: Count the points.
flow.say: Which clue was hardest? Which one would be different in Chennai?
flow.kid: Which clue was hardest? Which is different in Chennai?
flow.think: Is there a clue that happens in two seasons?

games.context: This is a matching game. Each living thing card goes with a problem the season brings, and with what they do about it.

printables.title: 10 living thing cards
items: Fisher family on the east coast

printables.title: 10 problem cards
items: The soil is dry for months, and leaves lose water all day.
My eggs need someone to hatch them while it is warm and food is plenty.
My eggs and tadpoles need water.
My lake freezes in winter, and I cannot reach the food.
I have few sweat glands, and summer afternoons are very hot.
I need to flower at the right time of year.
My rice needs a lot of water to grow.
The fish are breeding, and if we catch them now there will be fewer later.
I need a warm, sandy, safe place to lay my eggs.
In the snowy months there is almost no food.

printables.title: 10 answer cards
items: I take back the useful parts of my leaves and drop them, then grow new ones.
I lay my eggs in crows' nests in summer, and the crows raise my chicks.
I wait for the monsoon, then lay my eggs in the puddles.
I fly thousands of kilometres to a warm Indian lake.
I lie in mud or water to cool off.
I measure the nights, and flower when they are long.
I sow my seeds when the monsoon rains come.
We stop fishing at sea from 15 April to 14 June.
I come ashore on a beach from January to March and bury my eggs in the sand.
I eat a lot in autumn, then sleep in a den all winter.

rules: Lay all the cards face up in three rows: living things, problems and answers.
On your turn, pick one living thing card. Find their problem card and their answer card.
Say the set out loud as one sentence: who they are, what the season's problem is, and what they do.
If the others agree it is right, keep the set and score 1 point.
When all the sets are made, the player with the most sets wins. Playing alone, try to make all 10 sets in 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 30 cards. 2. Lay them in three rows, face up.
flow.say: Every living thing here has a problem that comes with a season. Can you find their problem, and what they do about it?
flow.kid: Lay out the cards in three rows. Match each living thing to a problem and an answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ready for the Season, a matching game about how living things cope with the seasons.

flow.do: Make the first set together, with the pintail duck.
flow.say: The pintail duck. Which problem is hers? And what does she do?
flow.kid: Find the pintail duck's problem and answer.

check.q: A pintail duck's lake in Central Asia freezes in winter. What does she do?
options: Flies thousands of kilometres to a warm lake in India
Sleeps under the ice
Eats the ice
check.why: When her lake freezes, she cannot reach the plants and small animals she eats. So she flies to India's lakes for the winter, and flies back in spring to lay her eggs. People once thought some birds slept under water in winter, but they really fly away.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to make sets. 2. Say each set as one sentence.
flow.say: Say each set as one sentence. For example: the neem tree's soil dries out, so she drops her leaves.
flow.kid: Make a set. Say it in one sentence. Who, what problem, what they do.
flow.parent: Every set starts with the living thing's own problem, then how their change helps them. Ask: which change happens in the body, and which is something they do?

flow.do: Count the sets and talk.
flow.say: Which of these changes is a journey? Which is a change in the body? Which is something people decided together?
flow.kid: Which is a journey? Which is a body change? Which did people decide?
flow.think: Which set is most like something your family does?

experiments.title: Hidden Colours: is there yellow inside a green leaf?
experiments.context: In this experiment you rub a green leaf and a yellowing leaf onto paper strips, and let a liquid carry their colours up the paper. You find out which colours each leaf was hiding.
experiments.question: A green leaf and a yellowing leaf: what colours does each one hold?
experiments.predict: Look at the green palak leaf and the yellowing palak leaf. When the liquid climbs the paper, what colours do you think each one will show? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind of paper strip for both leaves, the same coin and the same number of rubs, 10 for each. Draw both lines 2 cm from the bottom. Stand both strips in the same liquid, 1 cm deep, for the same time. Only the leaf changes.
results_table: Colours I saw, from bottom to top
How high did the top colour go (cm)?

materials.item: two fresh, dark green palak leaves. Coriander, amaranth or curry leaves also work.
one yellowing leaf: a palak or coriander leaf that has gone yellow in the fridge, or a yellow leaf from a potted plant
two strips of white blotting paper, about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long. No blotting paper? Use a white paper napkin folded into four layers, or a coffee filter.
nail polish remover, a few spoons. It works best if it says acetone on the label. Or rubbing alcohol, or liquid hand sanitiser (not gel).
a one-rupee or two-rupee coin
two small glass or steel tumblers, and two small plates or lids to cover them
a pencil, a ruler, cello tape and a notebook

experiments.safety: Nail polish remover catches fire very easily. Keep it far from any flame: no diya, stove, mosquito coil or agarbatti in the room. Open a window. A grown-up pours it, and nobody sniffs it. Keep the tumblers covered. Wash hands afterwards. Pour what is left down the sink with plenty of running water.

schedule.what: Rub a green leaf and a yellowing leaf onto paper strips. Stand them in nail polish remover for 20 minutes. Compare the colours.

experiments.record: Tape both dry strips into your notebook side by side. Label each colour band. Fill in the table.

flow.do: 1. Cut two strips of blotting paper, 2 cm wide and 12 cm long. 2. Draw a pencil line across each strip, 2 cm from the bottom. 3. Write 'green' at the top of one strip and 'yellow' at the top of the other, in pencil.
flow.say: We are going to find out if a leaf has colours we cannot see. First we make two paper strips, one for each leaf.
flow.kid: Cut two paper strips. Draw a line 2 cm from the bottom. Label them 'green' and 'yellow'.
flow.parent: Use pencil, not pen. Pen ink would run up the strip too and mix with the leaf colours.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hidden Colours. Here you make two paper strips to test a green leaf and a yellowing leaf.

flow.do: 1. Show both leaves. 2. Ask your child to guess what colours each will show on the strip, and why. 3. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: This leaf is green, and this one has gone yellow. When we let a liquid climb the strip, it can carry a leaf's colours up and spread them apart. What colours do you think each leaf will show? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at both leaves. What colours will each show? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What colours do you think the green leaf will show?
good: Only green, because it looks green.
Maybe some other colour hiding, because leaves go yellow later.

flow.parent: Don't say what will happen. Most children guess 'only green' for the green leaf and 'only yellow' for the yellow one. Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Lay the green palak leaf over the pencil line on the 'green' strip. 2. Roll the edge of the coin firmly along the line, pressing hard, so the leaf leaves a dark green line. 3. Move to a fresh part of the leaf and roll again. Do 10 rolls in all. 4. Do the same with the yellowing leaf on the other strip, also 10 rolls.
flow.say: Press the coin's edge down hard and roll it along the line. Each roll squeezes a little colour out of the leaf onto the paper. We do 10 rolls on each strip, so it's fair.
flow.kid: Put the leaf on the line. Roll the coin's edge hard along it. Do 10 rolls.
flow.parent: The green line should be dark and thin, just on the pencil line. A thick, dark line gives clearer colours. The yellowing leaf gives a paler line, and that is fine. Count the rolls out loud together.

flow.do: 1. Open a window. 2. Pour nail polish remover into each tumbler, just 1 cm deep. 3. Stand one strip in each tumbler, with the leaf line above the liquid. 4. Tape the top of the strip to the rim. 5. Cover each tumbler with a small plate.
flow.say: The leaf line must stay above the liquid, or the colours would wash off into it. The plate on top stops the liquid drying up.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the liquid. Keep the green line above it. Put a plate on top.
flow.parent: If the liquid is deeper than 2 cm, it will touch the leaf line and the colours will just dissolve into the tumbler. Pour less. Keep the bottle closed and away from any flame.

flow.do: 1. Watch the liquid climb the paper. 2. Every few minutes, look at the colours through the side of the tumbler. 3. After about 15 to 20 minutes, or when the liquid is 1 cm from the top, lift the strips out. 4. Mark the top of the liquid with a pencil. 5. Lay them on a plate to dry.
flow.say: Watch the line. What is happening to the green? Is any other colour moving away from it?
flow.kid: Watch the strip. Does the green move? Can you see another colour?
flow.parent: On the green leaf's strip, the green spreads up into a band, and a thin yellow or yellow-orange band runs ahead of it, near the top. On the yellowing leaf's strip, the yellow band is usually clear, and there is much less green, or none. The colours fade as the strip dries, so look at them straight away. If you see only green, the line was too faint. Make a new strip with 20 rolls, or let it run longer. Hand sanitiser works more slowly than nail polish remover.

check.q: On the green leaf's strip, a yellow band appeared above the green. Where did the yellow come from?
options: The liquid is yellow
The leaf had a yellow colour hidden under the green
The paper turned yellow when it got wet
check.why: The yellow came from the leaf. The liquid is clear, and the paper above the yellow band stays white. So the yellow was in the green leaf all along, hidden because the green is so strong. Picking the paper is a fair guess, but then the whole wet strip would be yellow.

flow.do: 1. Put the two strips side by side. 2. Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Put the strips side by side. What do you think now about the colours in a leaf? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think the yellowing leaf looked different?
flow.kid: Compare the strips. What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A strong answer sounds like this. What I think: a green leaf has yellow inside it too. What I saw: the green leaf made a green band and a yellow band. The yellowing leaf made a yellow band and hardly any green. Why: when a leaf gets old, the green goes first, and the yellow that was there is left. Now tell your child that trees do this before dropping leaves in the dry season, and take the useful parts of the green back.

check.q: The yellowing leaf showed a strong yellow band but little green. What does this tell you?
options: The leaf lost the green, and the yellow stayed
The leaf grew a lot of new yellow
Yellow leaves have no colour at all
check.why: Both leaves had the yellow band. The difference was the green: the yellowing leaf had lost most of it. So a leaf turns yellow because the green goes, and the yellow that was always there shows. Thinking the leaf grew new yellow is what most people guess, but the green leaf already had the yellow.

experiments.title: Straight or Slanting: how far does the same torchlight spread?
experiments.context: In this experiment you shine a torch on squared paper, straight down and then at a slant, and count the squares it lights. It shows why the high summer Sun warms the ground more than the low winter Sun.
experiments.question: Does the same torch light up more squares when it shines straight down, or at a slant?
experiments.predict: Will the patch of light be bigger when the torch shines straight down, or when it shines at a slant from the side? Will it be brighter or dimmer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same torch and the same squared paper every time. Keep the torch 20 cm from the middle of the patch, measured with a ruler. Only the angle changes. Do each angle twice, because a shaky hand can change the patch.

materials.item: a small torch with a narrow beam. A phone torch works too, but its patch is wider and fuzzier.
a page of squared paper from a maths notebook, or a sheet with 1 cm squares ruled on it
a 30 cm ruler, a pencil and cello tape
a pile of books, to rest the torch on
a room you can make dark, at night or with the curtains closed

experiments.safety: Never point the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Shine a torch on squared paper straight down, at a slant and very low. Count the squares lit each time.

experiments.record: Keep the paper with the three outlines drawn on it. Fill in the table, and draw a bar for each angle.

flow.do: 1. Tape the squared paper flat on the floor or a table. 2. Mark a small dot in the middle. 3. Make the room dark.
flow.say: This paper is the ground, and the torch is the Sun. We will shine the same torch at the same dot, from different angles.
flow.kid: Tape the paper down. Mark a dot in the middle. Turn off the lights.
flow.context: This is the first step of Straight or Slanting. You shine a torch on squared paper at different angles and count the squares it lights.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: First the torch will shine straight down. Then at a slant, like the Sun in the afternoon. Then very low, like the Sun near sunset. Which patch will be biggest? Which will be brightest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Straight down, a slant, or very low. Which patch is biggest? Why?
flow.parent: Don't give the answer. Some children think the light will be the same size every time, because it is the same torch.

flow.do: 1. Hold the torch straight above the dot, with the glass 20 cm from the paper. Use the ruler to check. 2. Your child draws round the edge of the bright patch in pencil. 3. Count the squares inside. Count a square if more than half of it is lit. 4. Do it twice.
flow.say: Hold still. Draw round the edge of the bright part. Now count the squares inside.
flow.kid: Shine straight down. Draw round the bright patch. Count the squares.
flow.parent: Rest your elbow on the table to keep the torch steady. The edge of the patch may be fuzzy. Draw round the edge of the brightest part each time, so the counts are fair.

flow.do: 1. Now hold the torch at a slant, half-way between straight down and flat, still 20 cm from the dot. Rest it on a pile of books to keep it still. 2. Draw round the patch and count. 3. Then hold the torch very low, nearly flat, still 20 cm from the dot. 4. Draw round the patch and count. Do each twice.
flow.say: The torch is the same distance from the dot. Only the angle has changed. Is the patch bigger or smaller? Is it brighter or dimmer?
flow.kid: Now shine at a slant. Then very low. Draw and count each patch.
flow.parent: The slanting patch is an oval, bigger than the straight one, and dimmer. The very low patch is a long oval, often two to three times the squares of the straight patch, and clearly dim. Your numbers depend on your torch, so they will not match anyone else's exactly.

check.q: The torch gave out the same light each time. When it shone at a slant, the patch was bigger. What happened to the light in each square?
options: Each square got less light, because the same light was spread over more squares
Each square got more light, because the patch was bigger
Each square got the same light
check.why: The same amount of light was spread over more squares, so each square got a smaller share. That is why the slanting patch looked dimmer. Thinking a bigger patch means more light is a common guess, but the torch did not get any stronger.

flow.do: 1. Look at the three outlines together. 2. Ask: what I think, what I saw, and why. 3. Then link it to the Sun.
flow.say: In summer, the Sun at noon is high, nearly straight above us. In winter, it is lower in the sky. Which torch was like the summer Sun? Which ground would get warmer?
flow.kid: Which torch was like the summer Sun? Which ground warms more?
flow.parent: A strong answer: what I think is that straight light warms the ground more. What I saw: the straight patch was smallest and brightest, and the low patch was biggest and dimmest. Why: the same light is packed into fewer squares when it falls straight down. The high summer Sun is like the straight torch. The days are also longer in summer, so the ground gets more hours of sunshine.

activities.title: Season Detectives: what season is it today?

materials.item: a window or balcony
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Stay inside the balcony railing. Don't lean out.

schedule.what: Look for clues of the season outside the window and inside the home. Decide which season it is.

activities.record: Draw a table with two columns: 'Clue' and 'What it tells me'. Write at least five clues.

flow.do: 1. Stand at a window or on the balcony together. 2. Look, listen and feel for one minute. 3. Then walk round the home and look for more clues: clothes drying, the fan, fruit in the kitchen, the calendar.
flow.say: We are season detectives. Without looking at the calendar, can you find five clues that tell us what season it is? Look outside, listen, and feel the air. Then look round the house.
flow.kid: Find five clues of the season. Look, listen, feel. Then look round the house.
flow.parent: Good clues: how hot or damp the air feels, whether the fan is on, the clothes people wear, rain or dry dust, the fruit in the kitchen, birds calling, a tree with or without leaves, how long your shadow is, and festivals coming up.
flow.context: This is a starting activity for the seasons unit. You look for clues that tell you what season it is right now.

flow.do: 1. Read the clues together. 2. Ask your child to name the season and say which clue was the strongest. 3. Ask what will be different in three months.
flow.say: So which season is it? Which clue made you most sure? What do you think will be different in three months' time?
flow.kid: Which season is it? Which clue is best? What will change in three months?

ask.q: Which clue is the best one, and why?
good: The mangoes, because they only come in summer.
The rain, because it only rains a lot in the monsoon here.

flow.parent: There is no single right clue. A strong answer gives a clue that only happens in one season, and says why.

activities.context: A starting activity: you look for clues outside and inside your home to work out the season.

activities.title: The Coconut Oil Season Test

materials.item: liquid coconut oil, 2 teaspoons
two small steel bowls
a fridge
a notebook

activities.safety: No safety risks. Wipe up any spilled oil so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Put one bowl of coconut oil in the fridge and leave one in the room. After 30 minutes, compare them.

activities.record: Draw both bowls after 30 minutes. Write what each one looks like.

flow.do: 1. Put one teaspoon of liquid coconut oil in each bowl. 2. Ask your child to guess what will happen in the fridge. 3. Put one bowl in the fridge, not the freezer. Leave the other in the room.
flow.say: In winter in Delhi, coconut oil goes white and hard in the bottle. Here is a small test. What do you think will happen to the oil in the fridge? Why?
flow.kid: One bowl goes in the fridge. One stays out. What will happen? Why?
flow.context: This activity uses coconut oil to feel the difference between a warm season and a cold one.

flow.do: 1. After about 30 minutes, take the bowl out of the fridge. 2. Compare the two bowls. Tip each one gently. 3. Then hold the cold bowl in your warm hands and watch.
flow.say: Look at both bowls. Tip them. What is different? Now hold the cold one in your hands. What happens?
flow.kid: Compare the bowls. Tip them. Hold the cold one. What happens?
flow.parent: The fridge oil turns white and solid, because coconut oil sets below about 24 degrees Celsius. In your warm hands, it melts back to clear liquid within a few minutes. If your room is cooler than about 24 degrees, both bowls may set. Then warm one bowl in your hands.

flow.do: Talk about where in India coconut oil goes solid, and when.
flow.say: In Chennai and Kochi, the bottle stays liquid almost all year. In Bengaluru it often sets on cool winter mornings. In Delhi, it sets for most of the winter. What does that tell us about winter in these places?
flow.kid: Where in India does coconut oil go hard? What does that tell you?

check.q: Meena's coconut oil in Delhi is hard and white in January. Kavya's oil in Kochi is clear and runny in January. Why?
options: January in Delhi is much colder than January in Kochi
Delhi's coconut oil is a different kind
Oil goes hard when it is old
check.why: Coconut oil sets when it is cooler than about 24 degrees Celsius. Delhi's winter is cold, and Kochi stays warm all year. The oil is the same. The season is different.

activities.context: In this activity, a little coconut oil shows how different winter is in different parts of India.

activities.title: Sun Patch on the Floor (if sunlight comes in through a window)

materials.item: a window that gets sunlight at some time of day
a strip of cello tape or masking tape, and a pen
a clock

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Mark the edge of the sun patch on the floor at the same time each week.

activities.record: Write the date on each tape mark. After a few months, draw where the patch has moved.

flow.do: 1. Choose a time when sunlight comes through the window onto the floor, for example 11 o'clock. 2. Stick a short strip of tape at the inner edge of the sun patch, the edge furthest into the room. 3. Write the date on the tape.
flow.say: The Sun's light makes a patch on our floor. If the Sun is lower in the sky, the light comes further into the room. Let's mark where the edge is today, at the same time every week.
flow.kid: Put tape at the edge of the sun patch. Write today's date on it.
flow.context: This is a slow activity for a home where sunlight comes in through a window. You mark the edge of the sun patch every week, and see it move with the season.

flow.do: 1. One week later, at the same time, mark the edge again. 2. Keep going every week for as long as you like. 3. Compare the marks.
flow.say: Is the patch further into the room or nearer the window than last week? What does that tell you about how high the Sun is now?
flow.kid: Mark the edge again. Has it moved in or out?
flow.parent: If the window faces south, in most of India the patch reaches deep into the room in December and January, when the midday Sun is low in the south. In April and May, the Sun is high and the patch stays near the window, or does not come in at all. The change from week to week is small, so it takes a month or more to see clearly.

activities.context: A slow activity for a sunny window: mark where the sunlight lands on your floor each week, and watch it move with the seasons.

activities.title: The Season Wheel: India's year in one circle

materials.item: a paper plate or a circle of card
crayons or sketch pens
a pencil and a ruler
a calendar

schedule.what: Make a wheel of the twelve months. Colour the seasons where you live, and add your family's festivals, foods and changes.

activities.record: Keep the wheel on the wall. Add to it as each month comes.

flow.do: 1. Draw lines to split the plate into 12 equal parts, like a pizza. 2. Write the months round the edge, starting with January at the top. 3. Colour the months: orange for summer, blue for the rains, green for the cool months.
flow.say: Let's make our year into a wheel. Which months are hot here? Which months are rainy? Which are cool?
flow.kid: Split the plate into 12 parts. Write the months. Colour the seasons.
flow.parent: Colour it for where you live. In Chennai, the big rains come from October to December. In Mumbai or Kochi, they come from June to September. If you are unsure, ask a grandparent.
flow.context: In this activity you make a season wheel, a circle of the twelve months with your seasons, foods and festivals on it.

flow.do: 1. In each month, draw or write one thing your family does or eats. 2. Add one plant and one animal you notice in that month.
flow.say: What do we eat in May? When is Pongal? When do we take out the umbrellas? When does the koel call?
flow.kid: Draw one food, one festival, one plant or animal in each month.
flow.parent: Examples: mangoes and nungu in May, umbrellas and frogs in the rains, Diwali sweets, sevanthi garlands in December, Pongal and sugarcane in January, neem flowers at Ugadi.

flow.do: Look at the finished wheel together.

flow.kid: December leads back to January. What does that tell you?
flow.think: Does a year have a beginning, or is it a circle?

projects.title: My Season Diary: one tree, four weeks

materials.item: a tree you can see from a window or balcony, or a potted plant at home
a notebook, pencil and crayons
a phone, to look up sunrise and sunset times

projects.safety: Stay inside the balcony railing. Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Choose your tree or plant. Draw them. Write the date, the weather, and the sunrise and sunset times.
Draw the same tree or plant again. Note any new leaves, falling leaves, flowers, fruit or visitors.
Draw and note again. Add any bird or insect you saw on or near the tree.
Draw a fourth time. Compare all four pages and write what changed.

projects.record: Four diary pages, one a week. Each has a drawing, the date, the weather, the sunrise and sunset times, and one change you noticed.

flow.do: 1. Choose one tree you can see from home, or a potted plant. 2. Draw the whole tree or plant. 3. Write the date and the weather. 4. Look up today's sunrise and sunset times, and work out the day length.
flow.say: We are going to watch one tree for four weeks, like a scientist. Every week, you draw them and write down what you see. Today is the first page.
flow.kid: Choose a tree. Draw them. Write the date, the weather and sunrise time.
flow.parent: A tree that is changing helps a lot: one dropping leaves, flowering or fruiting. In February to April, neem, peepal, gulmohar and the Indian almond often change fast. A potted plant works if you can't see a tree.
flow.context: This is the first day of a four-week project. You keep a diary of one tree or plant, once a week.

flow.do: 1. Draw the same tree from the same place. 2. Write the date, weather and sunrise and sunset times. 3. Write one change since last week.
flow.say: Look carefully. What is different from last week? New leaves? Fewer leaves? Flowers? A bird?
flow.kid: Draw the tree again. What is different from last week?

flow.do: Draw and write again. Add any animal you saw on or near the tree.
flow.say: Did you see any birds, squirrels or insects visiting the tree this week? What were they doing?
flow.kid: Draw again. Did any animal visit the tree? What did they do?

flow.do: 1. Draw a fourth time. 2. Lay all four pages side by side. 3. Write three changes you saw, and whether the days got longer or shorter.
flow.say: Put all four pages side by side. What changed in the tree? What changed in the day length? Do you think the two are linked?
flow.kid: Look at all four pages. What changed? Did the days get longer or shorter?

check.q: Ananya's diary from February to March shows her neem tree dropping yellow leaves, then growing new ones. What is the best reason?
options: The tree is changing with the dry season, as neem trees do every year
The tree is sick and then got better
Someone painted the leaves
check.why: Neem trees drop many old leaves in the dry months and grow new ones, often by Ugadi. It happens every year, so it is a seasonal change, not an illness.

challenges.title: Water for the Birds in May
challenges.problem: In the hottest weeks of summer, birds in the city struggle to find water. Design a water bowl for your balcony or window sill that birds can use safely, that stays cool and clean, and that does not tip over.
constraints: The water must be shallow, no deeper than 3 cm, so small birds cannot drown.
It must not tip over when a crow lands on the edge.
It must be easy to wash and refill every day.
materials: a shallow clay saucer from under a flower pot, or a wide steel plate
a few small stones or a brick
general: People put a shallow clay saucer of water in a shady corner of the balcony, and refill it every morning.
A few stones in the water give small birds a place to stand.
creative: Put the clay saucer inside a slightly bigger one with a little water between them, so it stays cool for longer.
Hang a second bowl under the edge of a sunshade, so it is in shade all afternoon.
Keep a diary of which birds come and at what time.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own bird water bowl. Draw it, build it, put it out, and record which birds visit in a week.

flow.do: Read the problem together and draw two ideas.
flow.say: Birds need water most in the hottest weeks, when puddles have dried up. What would make a bowl safe, cool and steady? Let's each draw two ideas.
flow.kid: Birds need water in summer. Draw two bowl ideas. Safe, cool and steady.
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You make a water bowl that helps city birds through the hot season.

flow.do: 1. Build the best idea. 2. Put it in a shady place on the balcony or window sill. 3. Press on the edge to test that it does not tip.
flow.say: Let's build it. Put it in the shade. Press on the edge like a crow landing. Does it stay steady?
flow.kid: Build it. Put it in the shade. Press the edge. Does it tip?
flow.parent: Clay keeps water cooler than steel, because a little water soaks through the clay and dries from the outside. Wash the bowl and change the water every day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas, and plan a week of watching.
flow.say: Here are some other ideas. Can you make yours better? Who do you think will come first?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Who will come first, do you think?

check.q: Why should the water in a bird bowl be changed every day?
options: So mosquitoes cannot lay eggs and breed in it
So it stays deep
So birds don't get bored
check.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the young take about a week to grow into adults. Changing the water every day stops them, and keeps it clean for the birds.

challenges.title: A Shade for Summer: keep the ice in a box (on a sunny balcony)
challenges.problem: In summer, people shade their windows and roofs to keep their homes cool. Design a shade for a shoebox house, so that an ice cube inside melts more slowly than one in a box with no shade, in the same sunshine.
constraints: Use only paper, card, cloth and things from home.
Both boxes must be the same, except for your shade.
Both boxes sit in the same sunshine for the same time.
You need sunshine on a balcony, terrace or window sill for about 40 minutes.
materials: two shoeboxes of the same size
two ice cubes of the same size, on two small steel plates
card, newspaper, an old white cloth, a coconut leaf or a sack
general: Make a roof of card that sticks out past the walls, like the deep sunshades over windows.
Cover the box with a white cloth, because white sends back more sunlight than dark colours.
creative: Leave a gap of air between the shade and the box, so the shade's heat doesn't touch the box.
Use a wet cloth as the shade, so it cools as it dries, like a wet khus curtain.
Copy a thatched roof with a coconut leaf.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own summer shade. Draw it, build it, test it against a box with no shade, and try to beat your first design.

flow.do: Read the problem and draw two shade ideas.
flow.say: How do homes in summer stop the Sun heating them? Think of sunshades, curtains and thatch. Draw two ideas for a shade for this box.
flow.kid: How do homes stay cool in summer? Draw two shade ideas.
flow.context: This is a design challenge for a sunny day. You make a shade that keeps an ice cube from melting fast in a shoebox.

flow.do: 1. Build the shade on one box. 2. Put an ice cube on a plate inside each box. 3. Put both boxes side by side in full sunshine. 4. Check every 10 minutes. 5. Note which ice cube is smaller.
flow.say: Both boxes are in the same sun. Only the shade is different. Check every 10 minutes. Which ice is melting slower?
flow.kid: Both boxes in the sun. Check every 10 minutes. Which ice melts slower?
flow.parent: The ice in the shaded box should stay bigger. If both melt at the same speed, the shade may be touching the box and passing its heat on. Try leaving a gap of air.

flow.do: Compare the ice cubes and read the other ideas.
flow.say: Which ice cube lasted longer? Why do you think your shade worked? How could you make it better?
flow.kid: Which ice lasted longer? Why? How could you make it better?

check.q: Why did the shaded box keep its ice longer?
options: The shade stopped much of the sunlight from reaching the box
The shade made cold
The ice in that box was colder to start
check.why: The shade took the sunlight before it reached the box, so less heat got in. A shade makes no cold. It only keeps the Sun's heat out. Both ice cubes were the same at the start, so that is not the reason.

setup.art: The two plates after 30 minutes: a small puddle and a small ice cube from the unshaded box, and a bigger ice cube from the shaded box.
