opts: A part of the year with its own kind of weather, which comes back every year
quiz.why: A season is a part of the year with its own weather, like summer or the rainy season. The seasons come back in the same order every year.

quiz.p: In most of India, which months are the main rainy season?
quiz.why: The south-west monsoon brings most of India's rain from June to September. Tamil Nadu is different: Chennai gets most rain from October to December.

quiz.p: Why does the ground get hotter at noon in summer than at noon in winter?
opts: The summer Sun is higher, so its light is packed into a smaller patch
The Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
There are more clouds in summer
quiz.why: The high summer Sun shines nearly straight down, like the straight torch, so its light is packed into a small patch. The Earth is in fact closest to the Sun in January. Picking 'closer' is the most common wrong idea.

quiz.p: In the torch test, what happened when the torch shone at a slant from the same distance?
opts: The patch got bigger and dimmer
quiz.why: The same light spread over more squares, so the patch was bigger and dimmer. Each square got less light.

quiz.p: In the Hidden Colours test, which colours came out of a fresh green leaf?
quiz.why: The green leaf made a green band and a yellow band. The yellow was in the leaf all along, hidden under the green.

quiz.p: Why do leaves often turn yellow before they fall?
opts: The tree breaks down the green, and the yellow that was there shows
The leaf is painted by the sun
Yellow is the colour of dry soil
quiz.why: Before dropping a leaf, the tree breaks down the green chlorophyll and takes useful nutrients back. The yellow pigments stay longer, so the leaf looks yellow.

quiz.p: Why do many trees in India drop their leaves from about February to May?
opts: The soil is dry, and leaves lose water all the time
It is too cold for leaves
quiz.why: In the dry months there is little rain, and leaves lose water every day. Dropping leaves helps a tree save water until the rains.

quiz.p: Pintail ducks come to India's lakes in winter. Why?
opts: Their own lakes in Central Asia freeze, so they cannot reach food
quiz.why: In winter, ice covers their northern lakes, so they cannot reach the plants and small animals they eat. They fly to India, where the lakes stay open.

quiz.p: Why do frogs lay their eggs in the rainy season?
opts: Their eggs and tadpoles need water, and the puddles fill then
It is too hot in winter
The rain washes the eggs clean
quiz.why: Frog eggs and tadpoles must live in water. The monsoon fills puddles and ponds, so that is when frogs call and lay eggs.

quiz.p: Which of these is something people in India do in summer?
opts: Drink buttermilk and wear cotton clothes
quiz.why: In the summer heat, people wear loose cotton and drink buttermilk to keep cool. Sweaters are for winter, and rice is sown in the rains.

quiz.p: Pongal, in Tamil Nadu, celebrates what?
opts: The first rain of the monsoon
quiz.why: Pongal, in mid-January, celebrates the harvest. The Pongal dish is cooked with the new rice.

quiz.p: What did Garner and Allard find out about plants?
opts: Many plants use the length of the day and night to know when to flower
Plants flower only when they are very big
Plants flower only in the rain
quiz.why: They gave tobacco plants short days by putting them in a dark hut each afternoon. The plants flowered in summer. So day length, and really night length, tells many plants the season.

quiz.p: Sevanthi flowers when the nights are long. When are the nights longest in India?
quiz.why: The nights are longest around 21 or 22 December, so sevanthi flowers in the cool months.

items.p: Sort these clues. Which season does each one belong to, in most of India?
items.a: see items
items.why: A strong sorter thinks about why each clue happens then: mangoes ripen in the heat, frogs need puddles, ducks come when their own lakes freeze.

items.p: Look out of your window today. Write three clues that tell you what season it is, and say what each one tells you.
items.a: Any three real clues with a reason, for example: 'The fan is on all day, so it is hot. The tree is bare, which means the dry season. Mangoes are in the kitchen, so it is summer.'
items.why: A strong answer uses clues the child really saw, and links each one to the season.

items.p: Kavya lives in Chennai. In which months does Chennai get most of its rain?
items.why: Chennai gets most of its rain from the north-east monsoon, from October to December. Most of the rest of India gets most rain from June to September. Picking June to September is right for Kochi or Mumbai, but not for Chennai.

items.p: In the torch test, the torch shone straight down and then at a slant, from the same distance. What happened to the patch of light at a slant?
items.why: At a slant, the same light spread over more squares, so the patch was bigger and each square got less light. That is why it looked dimmer.

items.p: Why is the ground hotter at noon in May than at noon in December? Use the torch test in your answer.
items.a: In May, the noon Sun is high, nearly straight above us, like the torch shining straight down. Its light is packed into a small patch, so each bit of ground gets a lot. In December, the Sun is lower, like the slanting torch, so the same light is spread over more ground. The days are also longer in May.
items.why: A strong answer compares the high Sun to the straight torch and the low Sun to the slanting torch, and says the light is packed or spread.

items.p: In the Hidden Colours test, a green palak leaf made a yellow band on the paper strip. What does this show?
opts: A green leaf has a yellow colour hidden under the green
The liquid turned the leaf yellow
The coin left a yellow mark
items.why: The yellow came out of the leaf. It was there all along, but the strong green hides it. The liquid is clear, and the coin leaves no colour of its own.

items.p: A tree that drops all or most of their leaves for part of the year is called a ____ tree.
items.why: Deciduous trees, such as teak and peepal, drop their leaves in the dry months and grow new ones later.

items.p: A neem tree dropping yellow leaves in March must be sick.
items.why: False. Neem trees drop many old leaves in the dry months every year, and grow new leaves and flowers soon after. A yellowing leaf in a potted plant can sometimes mean too much water, but a neem dropping leaves in March is a normal seasonal change.

items.p: Draw a tree in the rainy season and the same tree in the dry season. Label what is different.
items.a: Two drawings: one tree full of green leaves with wet ground, one with yellow leaves falling or bare branches and dry ground. Labels such as 'green leaves', 'yellow leaves falling', 'dry soil'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the leaves changing and the reason: dry soil in the dry season.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'Rainy season' and 'Dry season'.

items.p: Match each animal to what they do in a season.
pairs: calls and lays eggs in crows' nests in summer
flies to India for the winter
lies in mud on hot afternoons
lays eggs on Chennai beaches from January to March
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal changes what they do to fit a season: heat, water, cold or a safe time for eggs.

items.p: Pintail ducks fly thousands of kilometres from Central Asia to India every winter. What problem does this long journey solve for them?
items.a: In winter, the lakes in Central Asia freeze, so the ducks cannot reach the plants and small animals they eat under the water. India's lakes stay open and full of food, so they fly here and go back in spring to lay eggs.
items.why: A strong answer starts with the duck's own problem, frozen lakes and no food, and then says how flying to India helps.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one something people do in summer, or in winter?
items: sit in the sun at noon
items.a: see items
items.why: People change clothes and food to stay comfortable, and festivals often follow the harvest of each season.

items.p: Why do many families dry vadams and make pickles in summer?
opts: The strong summer sun dries food quickly
Vadams only taste good in summer
There is no rice in other seasons
items.why: Summer sunshine is strong and the air is dry, so food dries in hours. In the rains, food would stay damp and could go mouldy. The vadams then keep for months.

items.p: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
items.why: True. The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in India. This shows that being close to the Sun is not what makes summer.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 3, says: 'Summer is hot because the Earth is close to the Sun then.' Give one fact that shows she is wrong.
items.a: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, and that is winter in India. Or: when it is summer in India, it is winter in Australia, under the same Sun. So distance cannot be the reason.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real fact, not just 'it is the tilt', and says why the fact proves the idea wrong.

items.p: The green colouring in leaves, which plants use to catch sunlight, is called ____.
items.why: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that plants use to catch sunlight and make their food.

items.p: In the Hidden Colours test, Fatima's yellowing coriander leaf made a strong yellow band but almost no green. Her green leaf made both. What is the best explanation?
opts: The yellowing leaf had lost most of its green, and the yellow stayed
The yellowing leaf made new yellow
She did fewer coin rolls on the green leaf
items.why: Both leaves had the yellow. Only the green was different. So as a leaf ages, the green goes first, and the yellow that was always there shows. If she did the same 10 rolls on each, the number of rolls cannot be the reason.

items.p: Before a tree drops their leaves, they break down the green chlorophyll and move useful nutrients back into the branches. Why is this better for the tree than just dropping green leaves?
items.a: The leaves hold nutrients such as nitrogen, which the tree worked hard to take from the soil. If the tree dropped green leaves, those nutrients would be lost on the ground. By taking them back first, the tree can use them again for new leaves.
items.why: A strong answer says the nutrients are saved and reused, not wasted.

items.p: Sushila's family is looking at a peepal tree that is dropping leaves in March, in front of their building.

views.says: The tree is fine. Peepal trees drop their leaves every dry season and grow new pink ones.
The tree must be sick. We should call someone to cut it before it falls.
We can't be sure from one look. Let's watch the tree for a month and see if new leaves come.

items.ask: Whose idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence: peepal trees are deciduous and drop leaves in the dry season every year, so Sushila is probably right. It then gives another view its due: Amma's plan to watch is how a scientist would check, and Mr Rao is right that a sick tree can fall and hurt someone. So checking for other signs, such as rotten wood, is wise.
items.why: There is a real choice between knowing a pattern, checking with evidence, and being careful about safety. The best answers use the seasonal pattern and the idea of watching over time.

items.p: Rani does the torch test. Straight down, the torch lights 30 squares. Very low, it lights 90 squares. How much light does each square get when the torch is low, compared with straight down?
items.why: The same light is spread over 3 times as many squares, 90 instead of 30. So each square gets about a third of the light. That is why the low Sun of a winter evening feels weak.

items.p: Put these in order through one year for a teak tree in India, starting in the rains.
items: Full green leaves in the rains
Branches are bare in the dry months
a: Full green leaves in the rains
Branches are bare in the dry months
items.why: Teak is green in the rains. As the dry season comes, the leaves turn yellow and fall. The tree stands bare for a while, and then new leaves come out, often just before or with the next rains.

items.p: In Delhi, the longest day in June has about 14 hours of daylight. The shortest day in December has about 10. How might this help a plant know the season?
items.a: The days are long in June and short in December, and this happens the same way every year. A plant that can sense how long the nights are can tell whether it is the warm part of the year or the cool part, and flower at the right time.
items.why: A strong answer says that day length changes the same way every year, so it is a reliable clock, better than weather that can change from day to day.

items.p: Sevanthi, the chrysanthemum, flowers when the nights get long. When would you expect sevanthi flowers to be plentiful in the market?
items.why: The nights are longest around December, so sevanthi flowers then. That is why sevanthi garlands are cheap in the cool months.

items.p: Kochi and Chennai have a much smaller change between summer and winter than Delhi does.
items.why: True. Kochi and Chennai are near the equator, where the noon Sun is high all year, so their winters are mild. Delhi is further north, so its winter Sun is lower and its days shorter, and winter is much colder.

items.p: Draw the Sun at noon in May and at noon in December, over the same house. Draw the shadow of the house for each.
items.a: In May, the Sun is high, nearly overhead, and the shadow is very short. In December, the Sun is lower in the south, and the shadow is longer, pointing north.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the high Sun with a short shadow and the low Sun with a long shadow.
items.art: A small house on the ground, drawn twice, with empty sky above each.

items.p: A long journey that animals make every year at the same season is called ____.
items.why: Migration is a yearly journey, like the pintail duck's flight to India for the winter.

items.p: Sort these trees. Are they evergreen, green all year, or deciduous, dropping their leaves in the dry months?
items.a: see items
items.why: Coconut, mango and banana stay green all year. Teak, peepal and gulmohar drop their leaves in the dry season. Peepal is bare only for a short time.

items.p: The koel lays her eggs in crows' nests, and the crows raise her chicks. Why might summer be a good time for this?
items.a: In summer, crows are building nests and laying their own eggs too, so there are nests to use. Summer and the early rains also bring lots of food, such as fruit and insects, for the chicks.
items.why: A strong answer links the koel's plan to what the crows are doing in the same season, and to food for the young.

items.p: Every year, fishing at sea is stopped on the east coast from 15 April to 14 June. Why?
opts: Many fish breed then, so leaving them alone means more fish later
items.why: Many fish breed in these weeks. If they are caught then, fewer young fish are born, and there are fewer fish in the years after. The fishing ban protects them.

items.p: Match each ritu, from the old Indian calendar, with what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The six ritus split the year into two-month seasons. Vasanta is the time of Holi and Ugadi.

items.p: A girl in Class 3 says the yellow in a falling leaf is a new colour that the leaf makes as she dies. What would you show her to change her mind?
items.a: I would do the Hidden Colours test with a fresh green leaf. The green leaf also makes a yellow band on the strip. So the yellow was already in the leaf while it was green. It only shows when the green goes.
items.why: A strong answer uses the strip test as evidence, and explains that the yellow was there all along.

items.p: A shade on a window makes cold air for the room.
items.why: False. A shade makes no cold. It stops sunlight from reaching the window and the room, so less heat gets in.

items.p: Two scientists in the 1920s are arguing about why a tobacco plant flowered only in winter.

views.who: A scientist who trusts the old idea
views.says: Plants flower when they are big enough and old enough. This plant just needs more time.
The plant can tell the length of the day. Give it short days in summer, and it will flower.

items.ask: Which scientist do you side with? What test would you use to decide? Then say what the other scientist got right.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Garner and gives his test: shut some plants in a dark hut each afternoon to make their days short, keep others outside, and see which flower. It then says what the first scientist got right: many plants do need to reach a certain size before they can flower at all.
items.why: Both ideas can be partly true. Garner and Allard showed that day length decides when many plants flower. But a seedling that is too young often cannot flower yet, whatever the day length.

items.p: Garner and Allard's tobacco plants flowered when they were shut in the dark every afternoon. Later scientists found that a short flash of light in the middle of the night stopped them flowering. What does this tell you the plant is really measuring?
items.a: The plant is measuring how long the dark lasts without a break, the length of the night. A flash in the middle splits the long night into two short nights, so the plant acts as if the nights are short.
items.why: A strong answer says the plant measures the night, and explains why the flash matters: it breaks the night into two short ones.

items.p: Street lights shine all night near some trees in a city. What might happen to a plant that uses night length to know when to flower?
opts: It might flower at the wrong time, or not at all
It will flower twice as much
Nothing, because plants only feel daytime light
items.why: Bright light at night can make the night seem short to a plant. A plant that flowers in long nights might then flower late, or not at all. Scientists have found street lights can change when some plants flower and when their leaves fall.

items.p: In Australia, the summer holidays are in December and January. Use what you know about the tilted Earth to explain why.
items.a: The Earth's axis is tilted. In December, the southern half of the Earth, where Australia is, leans towards the Sun. The Sun is high there and the days are long, so it is summer. India's half leans away then, so India has winter.
items.why: A strong answer uses the tilt and says that the two halves of the Earth lean towards the Sun at opposite times of year.

items.p: Shreya repeats the torch test, but she holds the torch twice as far away for the slanting shine. Why is this not a fair test?
opts: Two things changed: the angle and the distance
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the distance changes too, she cannot tell whether the bigger patch came from the slant or from the extra distance.

items.p: Painting a leaf's yellow pigment on paper would turn the paper green over time.
items.why: False. The yellow pigment stays yellow. A leaf looks green only because she has much more green chlorophyll than yellow pigment. The yellow is always there underneath.

items.p: A neem tree in Hyderabad, from February to April. Put the changes in order.
items: Tiny white flowers open, ready for Ugadi pachadi
Old leaves turn yellow and fall
Reddish buds appear at the twig tips
Soft pale-green new leaves hang down
a: Old leaves turn yellow and fall
Reddish buds appear at the twig tips
Soft pale-green new leaves hang down
Tiny white flowers open, ready for Ugadi pachadi
items.why: The neem drops old leaves in the dry months, then buds open into new leaves, then the flowers come, often around Ugadi in March or April.

items.p: Old Indian calendars have six seasons. The weather department has four. Many people in Chennai say there are really three: hot, hotter and rainy. Which count would you choose for where you live, and why?
items.a: Any choice with a reason from local weather. For example: 'For Chennai, I would choose three: hot from March to June, the rains from October to December, and a cooler, drier time in January and February, because those are the biggest changes.'
items.why: A strong answer understands that seasons are a way of splitting the year, and chooses the split that fits the real weather of a place.

items.p: A scientist wants to find out if mango trees in Tamil Nadu are flowering earlier than 50 years ago. What would help most?
opts: Old written records of flowering dates, year after year
A photo of one mango tree today
Asking one person which month they like best
items.why: To see a change over 50 years, you need records from 50 years ago to compare with today. A single photo or one opinion cannot show a change over time.

items.p: Draw a picture that explains why a deciduous tree drops their leaves in the dry season. Show the soil, the roots, the leaves and the water.
items.a: Dry soil with little water near the roots, and many leaves losing water through tiny holes, with arrows showing water leaving. A second picture of the bare tree losing much less water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that leaves lose water, that the dry soil cannot replace it, and that fewer leaves means less water lost.
items.art: An empty box with a line for the ground near the bottom.

items.p: Buffaloes lie in mud on hot afternoons, but cows usually stand in the shade. Buffaloes have fewer sweat glands than cows. Explain why the mud helps a buffalo more than a cow.
items.a: Sweat cools a body as it dries. A buffalo has few sweat glands, so she cannot cool herself well by sweating. Wet mud on her skin dries slowly and cools her, like sweat would. A cow sweats more, so shade is often enough for her.
items.why: A strong answer starts with the buffalo's problem, few sweat glands in the heat, and explains how wet mud cools as it dries.

items.p: Olive ridley turtle eggs take about 50 days to hatch in the warm sand. Eggs laid on 20 February would hatch around:
items.why: February has 28 days in most years, so 8 days take us to the end of February. March has 31 days, which makes 39. 11 more days into April makes 50. So about 11 April.

items.p: Sort these changes. Is each one a change in the body, or a change in what the living thing does?
items: a neem tree's leaves turn yellow
a pintail duck flies to India
a Himalayan bear's body slows down in the den
a dog grows a thicker coat in a cold place
items.a: see items
items.why: Some living things change their bodies with the season, and others change what they do. Many do both.

items.p: The way plants use the length of the night to tell the season is called ____.
items.why: Garner and Allard named it photoperiodism in 1920. 'Photo' means light, and 'period' means a length of time.

items.p: The yellow was hidden in the green leaf all along. Think of something else that is hidden until something else goes away. Explain how it is like the leaf.
items.a: Any good example with a clear link. For example: stars are in the sky all day, but we see them only when the bright sunlight goes away at night. Like the yellow in the leaf, they were there all along, hidden by something brighter.
items.why: A strong answer finds a real example where something stronger hides something that was there all along, and explains the link.

applications: Farmers decide when to sow by the season. Rice is sown with the monsoon, and wheat in the cool months.
The weather department forecasts when the monsoon will reach Kerala, so farmers and cities can plan.
Flower growers use lamps at night to stop sevanthi flowering too early, or black covers to make it flower sooner.
Builders put deep sunshades over windows, so the high summer Sun is kept out and the low winter Sun comes in.
Solar panels are tilted to face the Sun, so its light falls on them as straight as possible.
The 61-day fishing ban protects fish while many of them breed.
Bird sanctuaries such as Vedanthangal and Pulicat are protected most carefully in the winter, when the visiting birds are there.
Families plan holidays, weddings, house painting and pickle-making around the seasons.
Doctors watch for mosquito-borne illnesses such as dengue in and after the rains, when mosquitoes breed fast.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a plant combine the length of the night, warmth and other signals into one choice to flower?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the substances involved, but how they all work together is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How are India's seasons changing as the Earth warms?
open_questions.why_open: There are fewer long records in India than in some countries. Scientists are still working out how much the rains and flowering times have shifted.

open_questions.q: How do migrating birds find the same lake in India every winter, after flying thousands of kilometres?
open_questions.why_open: Birds seem to use the Sun, the stars, the Earth's magnetism and landmarks. How they put these together is not fully known.

open_questions.q: Exactly when, and why, does the monsoon start each year?
open_questions.why_open: Forecasts of the monsoon's arrival have become much better, but they can still be off by days, and the reasons for each year's timing are still studied.

open_questions.q: Do young trees and old trees of the same kind feel the dry season coming in the same way?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find young and old trees drop and grow leaves at slightly different times. The reasons are not well understood.

maths.problem: In the torch test, Divya's torch lit 40 squares when it shone straight down. When it shone very low, the same light lit 120 squares. How many times as many squares did the low torch light? What share of the light did each square get?
maths.answer: 3 times as many squares. Each square got about a third of the light.
maths.explain: 120 divided by 40 is 3. The same light was shared among 3 times as many squares, so each square got a third as much. That is why the low light looked dim.
maths.context: This is about the Straight or Slanting test, where you shine a torch on squared paper at different angles.
maths.why_maths: Sharing the same light among more squares shows exactly how much weaker slanting light is.

maths.problem: In Delhi, the longest day in June has about 14 hours of daylight, and the shortest day in December has about 10 hours. In Chennai, the longest day has about 12 hours 50 minutes, and the shortest about 11 hours 20 minutes. How much longer is the longest day than the shortest, in each city?
maths.answer: Delhi: about 4 hours longer. Chennai: about 1 hour 30 minutes longer.
maths.explain: Delhi: 14 hours take away 10 hours is 4 hours. Chennai: from 11 hours 20 minutes, add 40 minutes to reach 12 hours, then 50 more minutes to reach 12 hours 50 minutes. 40 + 50 = 90 minutes, which is 1 hour 30 minutes. So the seasons change the day length much more in Delhi, which is further from the equator.
maths.context: This is about day length, the hours of daylight from sunrise to sunset, which changes with the seasons.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows why Delhi's seasons feel so much stronger than Chennai's.

maths.problem: Every year, fishing at sea on the east coast stops from 15 April to 14 June, both days included. How many days is that?
maths.explain: April: from 15 to 30 is 16 days. May has 31 days. June: from 1 to 14 is 14 days. 16 + 31 + 14 = 61 days.
maths.context: This is about the yearly fishing ban, which lets many fish breed in peace.
maths.why_maths: Counting days on a calendar shows how long the fish are left alone in their breeding season.

maths.problem: The weather department splits the year into four seasons: winter is 2 months, summer is 3 months, the south-west monsoon is 4 months and the post-monsoon season is 3 months. What fraction of the year is the south-west monsoon? Which two seasons together make half the year?
maths.answer: The monsoon is 4 out of 12 months, which is one third of the year. Summer and the post-monsoon season together make 6 months, half the year.
maths.explain: 4 out of 12 is the same as 1 out of 3, because 12 is 3 lots of 4. Half of 12 months is 6. Summer (3) and post-monsoon (3) make 6. Winter (2) and the monsoon (4) also make 6.
maths.context: This is about India's four seasons, as the India Meteorological Department counts them.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how big a share of the year each season takes.

maths.problem: Olive ridley turtle eggs take about 50 days to hatch in warm sand. Lakshmi's family sees a turtle lay eggs on a Chennai beach on 20 February. About when should the babies come out? February has 28 days this year.
maths.explain: From 20 February to the end of February is 8 days. March has 31 days, so that makes 39. 50 take away 39 is 11, so 11 days into April: about 11 April. The real time can be a week or more longer or shorter, depending on how warm the sand is.
maths.context: This is about olive ridley turtles, who lay their eggs on Indian beaches from about January to March.
maths.why_maths: Counting on through the calendar lets turtle volunteers know when to watch for babies.

roots.context: We have pulled hidden colours out of a leaf, watched light spread at a slant, and met the animals and people who change with the year. Now we ask what the seasons tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your strip drew a yellow band out of a leaf that looked only green. The yellow was there all along, hidden under the green. Before a tree drops leaves in the dry season, they break down the green and take back what is useful. Then the hidden yellow shows, and the leaf falls.
deep_truth.habit: We say a leaf 'turns' yellow, as if a new colour is painted on as the leaf dies. And we read yellow leaves as a sign of a sick tree. In the dry season, the yellow is the colour that was always there, showing once the tree has taken back the green.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Hidden Colours test, the green palak leaf gave a green band and a yellow band. The yellowing palak leaf gave a strong yellow band and much less green. Scientists have measured that trees take back about half of the nitrogen from their leaves before the leaves fall.

three.who_am_i: You change with the seasons too: your clothes, your food, even how long you sleep in the light evenings.
three.what_is_life: A tree feels the dry months coming, takes back what she needs from her leaves, and lets them go to grow new ones.
three.what_is_this_world: One tilted Earth going round one Sun gives every place its own pattern of seasons, and every living thing fits into it.

roots.thread: There is one Sun, and one Earth going round it, tilted the same way all year. From that one simple tilt come summer, the rains and the cool months, different in every place. And from each season come many answers: the neem drops her leaves, the koel calls, the frog sings in the puddle, the farmer sows rice, the duck flies south. Each living thing meets the same turning year in their own way.

teachings.teaching: There is a time for everything, and a season for every activity under the heavens. A time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to pull up what is planted.
teachings.link: In this unit, every living thing has their time: the sevanthi flowers in the long nights, the frog lays eggs in the rains, and the farmer sows with the monsoon.

teachings.teaching: All things grow and flourish, and then each one goes back to their root. Going back to the root is stillness.
teachings.link: Before a tree drops a leaf, she takes the useful nutrients back into her branches. In the dry season, she goes quiet and holds on to what she needs, until it is time for new leaves.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: the main investigation uses palak or coriander, which most kitchens have, and a yellowing leaf from the fridge, so no tree or garden is needed. The coin-roll method avoids grinding leaves. Nail polish remover with acetone gives the clearest bands in about 15 minutes. Rubbing alcohol and liquid hand sanitiser work more slowly, and plain water hardly moves the green, so it is not offered. The liquid must be shallower than the leaf line, or the colours simply wash off, so the step says 1 cm deep and a line at 2 cm. The yellow band can be thin and fades as the strip dries, so the steps say to look straight away and to use 20 rolls if the line is faint. Nail polish remover catches fire easily, so the steps keep it far from diyas, stoves and agarbattis, with a window open and an adult pouring. The torch test needs only a dark room, a torch and a maths notebook. Its numbers depend on the torch, so the example results are marked as made up. The sun patch activity and the shade challenge need sunshine, so they are marked 'if sunlight comes in' and kept out of the spine. The coconut oil test works only if the room is warmer than about 24 degrees, so the step says what to do if both bowls set. The spine is the season detective activity, Hidden Colours, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: About 1906, farmers in Maryland, in the United States, found a new kind of tobacco plant. It grew huge, taller than a man, but it would not flower in the summer, so it gave no seeds. People thought plants flowered when they were old enough or big enough, or when the weather was warm. This plant broke that idea. It was big, warm and well fed, and still did not flower. Then farmers noticed it did flower in winter, in a glasshouse. Wightman Garner and Harry Allard, two scientists in the United States government's farm department, wondered if the plant could tell the length of the day. In 1918 they tested it. Every afternoon they pushed some plants into a dark hut, so their days were short, like winter days. Other plants stayed outside. In the middle of summer, the plants with short days flowered, and the others did not. They published their results in 1920 and called this photoperiodism. In 1938, Karl Hamner and James Bonner showed that a short flash of light in the middle of the night could stop such plants from flowering. So what plants really measure is the length of the night.
how_we_found_out.who: Wightman Garner and Harry Allard, scientists in the United States Department of Agriculture, and later Karl Hamner and James Bonner
how_we_found_out.when: 1918 to 1920, with the night-length experiments in 1938
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a plant flowers when they are old enough, big enough or warm enough. Garner and Allard showed that many plants flower when the days reach a certain length, by shortening the days of tobacco plants with a dark hut. Later work showed that the plants are really measuring the length of the night.
